summary: Profiles X.509 v3 certificates and v2 CRLs for use on the Internet. It was replaced by RFC 5280.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a common Internet profile for X.509 public-key certificates and certificate revocation lists. It also explains how software can check a chain of certificates before trusting a public key.

questions: what is the internet x509 pki profile
what is in an x509 certificate
how does certification path validation work
subtitle: An Internet profile for X.509 certificates, revocation lists, and trust-path checks.

tldr.problem: Internet applications need certificates and revocation information that different implementations can interpret consistently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC profiles X.509 version 3 certificates and version 2 certificate revocation lists, and describes how to validate a certification path.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3280 was obsoleted by RFC 5280, which provides its replacement profile.

today: RFC 3280 is obsoleted by RFC 5280, which replaces its Internet certificate and CRL profile.

sections.title: An Internet Public-Key Infrastructure
sections.content:
A public-key certificate binds a public key to a named person or system. A trusted certification authority (CA) signs the certificate, and the certificate includes a limited validity period that a client can check independently.

The RFC profiles X.509 certificates and revocation lists for Internet applications such as web services, email, and IPsec. It aims to make common certificate information and validation behavior more interoperable without requiring one directory or delivery system.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate connects a public key to the person or system named in it. This RFC sets shared rules for certificates and their checking so Internet software can interpret them consistently.

sections.title: Certificate Fields and Extensions
sections.content:
The profile uses the X.509 version 3 certificate format. A certificate contains the information to be signed, the signing algorithm, and the signature; the signed information includes items such as a serial number, issuer, subject, validity, and public-key data.

Version 3 extensions add optional structured information such as alternative names, key usage, certificate policies, and limits on names or certification paths. The RFC specifies which extensions Internet implementations are required to support and how they are used.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate records who issued it, who or what it names, its public key, and when it is valid. Extensions add information about permitted uses and limits on the certificate.

sections.title: Building and Checking a Certification Path
sections.content:
A user may not already know the public key of the CA that signed a certificate. In that case, additional CA certificates form a certification path from a key the user trusts to the certificate being checked.

The RFC gives a detailed path-validation procedure. It checks certificate signatures and validity and processes constraints and policies along the path. Implementations must reach the same result, though they do not have to use the exact procedure in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: A certification path is a chain connecting a certificate to a CA key the user already trusts. Software checks the signatures, dates, and limits along that chain before accepting the public key.

sections.title: Revocation and Certificate Status
sections.content:
A CA can revoke a certificate before its validity period ends, for example when the subject's status changes or its private key may be compromised. A certificate revocation list (CRL) is a signed, dated list of revoked certificate serial numbers.

A client checks a suitably recent CRL when it uses a certificate. Because a new CRL is issued periodically, a revocation may not reach clients until a later update. The profile describes CRLs but does not require every deployment to issue them; online status methods are also possible.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can be revoked before its stated end date. A client can check a signed list of revoked certificates, but it may not learn about a new revocation until the list is updated.

sections.title: Limits of the Profile
sections.content:
The profile supports a broad baseline for Internet applications but does not remove the need to assess certificate policy or trust. The RFC notes that specialized environments may need added or replacement rules.

RFC 3280 obsoletes RFC 2459 and was itself later obsoleted by RFC 5280. Its security model depends on applications selecting trusted CA keys and applying the specified validation and revocation checks.
sections.plainLanguage: Following the profile does not decide whom an application should trust; that choice still depends on its policy and trusted CA keys. RFC 5280 later replaced this RFC.
